In principle yes. But two important challenges: (1) ensuring that these councils are truly independent (very difficult); (2) making sure that they do not appear as "technocratic overreach", with an agenda imposed from above (even more difficult).

column8: The process will be more politicized and not driven by economic/social considerations alone.
column11: The outcome depends greatly on the institutional framework and the composition and independence of the fiscal councils.

"Independent" councils are not necessarily independent. Rules are less subject to political interference, But the political process also seems important to sustaining agreement among legal sovereigns. I'm uncertain which would be preferred.

column5: This provides some useful information, but predicting crises is really hard, so that is a very high bar.
column8: The existing rules are pretty ineffective and keep having to be revised.  A reboot is a good idea.  See though the answer to the next question
column11: Having an independent group would likely be better.  All of these options can be politicized so the details of how the arrangements are structured matter greatly.

Fiscal councils would be a plus. However, fiscal councils should base their recommendations in part on a DSA -- these are complements not substitutes (or alternatives). So I do not agree with the tacit premise of this question.

column5: Depends on what the comparison is. Relative to existing EU rules, I think so.
